conversation.text: Explain the difference between mutable and immutable Python objects. Give one bug that shared mutable state can cause.

Lists and dictionaries are mutable; their contents can change in place. Strings and integers are immutable. Two names can refer to the same list, so appending through one name changes what the other sees. A mutable default list is reused across function calls and leaks old items. Use None as the default and create a fresh list inside each call.
Good explanation of mutable vs immutable objects and a real shared-state bug. How would you modify a function to avoid reusing a mutable default argument?

conversation.question: How would you modify a function to avoid reusing a mutable default argument?
conversation.answerAnchor: Two names can refer to the same list, so appending through one name changes what the other sees.

conversation.text: Use def add(value, items=None), then if items is None create items = [], append value and return items. Each call without items gets a fresh list. The old default list was one mutable object shared across calls; rebinding immutable objects such as strings cannot mutate that list.
